strengths: DRE-BO-SSL offers a useful, well-motivated combination of classification-based Bayesian optimization and graph-based semi-supervised learning. Using candidate geometry without additional objective evaluations is particularly appealing for fixed-pool optimization.

The experiments show substantial improvements over direct BORE/LFBO competitors on several problems, especially NATS-Bench and synthetic benchmarks. Comparisons against four classifier families and GP-based methods support weak acceptance as an empirical methodological contribution.

Twenty repeated runs, shared initialization settings, and reported standard errors strengthen the empirical evidence. The investigations of bandwidth, threshold ratio, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling provide useful information about practical behavior.

The paper clearly connects its construction to prior density-ratio estimation and semi-supervised learning methods. Pseudocode and benchmark descriptions facilitate understanding, and the appendix appropriately acknowledges limitations of applying existing theory to sequential optimization.
weaknesses: The central attribution to unlabeled data is not adequately isolated. Figure 12 includes a useful no-transductive baseline, but fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn beta; removing unlabeled data sometimes matches or improves performance. Matched comparisons controlling bandwidth selection and acquisition tie-breaking are needed to distinguish benefits of semi-supervision from the kernel classifier and other implementation choices.

The exploration explanation remains heuristic. Sampling truncated Gaussians around observed inputs does not ensure that high-density regions respect labels defined by a changing objective threshold. Appendix D cites results whose assumptions explicitly do not apply here, and provides no argument establishing that the proposed updates enlarge useful search regions. These limitations warrant qualifying the stronger mechanism and superiority statements.

Important implementation details remain unclear, including input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, bandwidth-optimization initialization and bounds, and acquisition selection from finite pools. The general description of 1,000-start L-BFGS-B also needs reconciliation with piecewise-constant tree acquisitions. These choices can materially affect both reproducibility and comparison fairness.

Evidence for broader applicability is limited. Continuous optimization is evaluated only on four two-dimensional functions. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses embeddings pretrained on 440,000 examples with the exact digit labels defining the optimization objective, providing substantial task-specific supervision. This supports structured-pool search more directly than general high-dimensional black-box optimization. A random-search baseline would also help contextualize the pool results.

Computational tradeoffs are insufficiently established. Dense graph construction, repeated propagation, and bandwidth fitting can be costly. Figure 14 usefully examines subsampling, but uses fixed bandwidth and does not compare complete optimization overhead against the baselines under the main adaptive-bandwidth configuration.
